INVESTOR UPDATE BUILDER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Write this month's investor update in five minutes

Enter MRR, customers and cash for the last few months. The tool works out growth, net burn, runway and burn multiple, tests whether you are default alive, and writes the update email with your highlights, lowlights and asks. Nothing leaves your browser.

New to the jargon? Burn multiple and default alive, with a worked example.

1. The numbers

One row per month, oldest first, the last row being the month you are reporting. Three or four months is plenty.

This month's MRR movements (optional, for quick ratio and churn)

2. The story, one point per line

Fill in the numbers, then click Build the update.

Your metrics

MonthMRRGrowthCustomersCashNet burn

The update

How it is built

Net burn: last month's cash minus this month's cash, plus any money raised that month. The headline figure averages the last three months.

Runway: cash divided by average net burn, and the month the cash would run out.

Burn multiple: this month's net burn divided by net new ARR (net new MRR times twelve).

Default alive: revenue grows at the compound monthly rate of the last three months, expenses stay flat at today's level, and the test asks whether revenue overtakes expenses before cash goes below zero within five years. A bisection finds the smallest growth rate that would pass.

Checked: the test suite recomputes the worked example by hand and runs hundreds of random histories, asserting that runway times burn equals cash, that being alive is monotone in growth, and that the required growth rate sits exactly on the boundary.

Common questions

What should go in a monthly investor update?

Investors want the same few things every month: the headline numbers (MRR, customers, cash, burn and runway), what went well, what went badly, and specific asks. A short update sent on a steady schedule builds more trust than a long one sent when there is good news. This tool turns your numbers into the metrics block and leaves room for your own highlights, lowlights and asks.

How do I calculate runway?

Runway is cash in the bank divided by net monthly burn, where net burn is the cash you lose each month after revenue, excluding money raised. This tool averages the last three months of burn so one unusual month does not swing the answer, and shows the month the cash would run out.

What is a good burn multiple?

The burn multiple is net burn divided by net new ARR. Under 1 is considered amazing, 1 to 1.5 great, 1.5 to 2 good, 2 to 3 suspect and over 3 bad. It tells an investor how much cash you spend to add a dollar of recurring revenue.

What does default alive mean?

A company is default alive if, at its current growth rate and with expenses held flat, revenue overtakes expenses before the cash runs out. Default dead means it will run out first unless something changes. The tool runs that projection from your numbers and also reports the monthly growth rate you would need to be default alive.

Is my data uploaded?

No. Everything is calculated in your browser, there are no accounts, and nothing is sent to a server. Use Save update to keep your numbers as a file and load them next month.

Is this financial advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type and a plain-text template. Check your figures before sending them to anyone, and follow your own legal obligations to investors.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type and a text template, not legal, financial, tax or securities advice. Check every figure before you send it to anyone; what you tell your investors is your responsibility. Independent. Not affiliated with any accelerator, investor or investor-reporting service, and none is named or ranked here.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you enter, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere, so use Save update and keep the file.

Everything runs in your browser. Revenue and cash figures are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (update_built, example_loaded, text_copied, markdown_copied, csv_downloaded, file_saved) are counted only in local storage on your device, never with any of your inputs, and are never sent anywhere. Switching them off below removes them and stays off on your next visit.

Related tools: the SaaS efficiency metrics calculator, the cash runway planner and the MRR waterfall calculator.

what-is-a-burn-multiple.html.text:
← Investor update builder

What is a burn multiple? Runway and default alive, with an example

Investors read a startup update for three answers: how fast revenue is growing, how long the cash lasts, and how much cash it costs to grow. Runway, burn multiple and the default-alive test are the three numbers that answer them. Here they are worked on four months of figures.

Open the free update builder

The example

MonthMRRCash in bank
June$20,000$400,000
July$22,000$380,000
August$24,200$355,000
September$26,600$325,000

Step 1: net burn

Net burn is the cash lost in a month. July lost $20,000, August $25,000 and September $30,000. The average of the last three months is $25,000 a month.

Step 2: runway

Runway is cash divided by net burn: $325,000 ÷ $25,000 = 13.0 months, so the cash lasts until about October 2027.

Step 3: burn multiple

MRR grew by $2,400 in September, which is $28,800 of net new annual recurring revenue. September's burn of $30,000 ÷ $28,800 = 1.04. Between 1 and 1.5 is usually called great: the company spends about a dollar to add a dollar of recurring revenue.

Step 4: default alive

MRR grew at a compound rate of +10.0% a month over the last three months. Hold expenses flat at today's level (MRR of $26,600 plus $25,000 of burn is $51,600 a month) and keep growing at that rate, and revenue overtakes expenses in about 7 months, around April 2027, well inside the 13 months of cash. The company is default alive. It would stay alive with growth of only 2.8% a month.

Frequently asked

How do I calculate burn multiple?

Divide net burn for the month by net new annual recurring revenue, which is net new MRR times twelve. $30,000 of burn against $2,400 of net new MRR is $30,000 divided by $28,800, a burn multiple of 1.04.

What is default alive?

A company is default alive if, at its current growth rate and with expenses held flat, its revenue overtakes its expenses before the cash runs out. The idea comes from Paul Graham's essay of the same name.

Why use the average of three months of burn?

One month of burn can be distorted by an annual prepayment, a large invoice or a one-off purchase. Averaging the last three months gives a steadier runway figure.
